wine.name: Quintet
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, about half the vineyard, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Malbec and Petit Verdot; the share of each moves with the season.
wine.sites: The house's own vineyard on a north facing hillside above Coldstream, on the Lilydale side of the valley, planted from 1971 to the five Bordeaux red varieties and farmed with compost and cover crops.
wine.making: Each variety is fermented on its skins for about twelve to fourteen days. The wine then matures for about twenty two months, roughly a quarter in large casks of fifteen hundred litres and more, nearly a third in new barriques and the rest in barriques two to five years old, and is bottled with little fining or filtration.
wine.glass: Red cherry, cassis and violet with a touch of clove and sweet French oak, leafier in cool years; medium in body, its line set by fine, firm tannin and fresh acidity rather than by weight of fruit.
wine.ageing: Tight on release and built to age: the house's own notes on vintages a decade and more old find tannin and acid for further keeping.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The five Bordeaux red varieties of the vineyard blended in one wine, hence the name.
The Geographical Indication on the label, the region north east of Melbourne where every grape was grown.

records.table: Mount Mary's Quintet is a Yarra Valley blend of the five Bordeaux red grapes from a hillside first planted in 1971. Red cherry, violet and fine, firm tannin at moderate weight make it a quiet wine for the cellar; decant it and pour it with lamb.
records.story: The Yarra Valley's first vines went in at Yering in 1838, and by 1921 the last of its old vineyards had been pulled out. Fifty years later a Melbourne doctor, John Middleton (1924 to 2006), and his wife bought a north facing hillside above Coldstream. They planted it in 1971, and the estate became one of the first vineyards of the valley's revival. By the house's account the first commercial release of Quintet came in 1976. The estate wines took two French shapes: two Bordeaux blends, the red Quintet and the white Triolet, and two Burgundy varieties, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. The wines were made in a restrained way, moderate in alcohol and gentle in extraction, and the house has held to that style. The founder died in June 2006, and the house dedicated its 2006 vintage to him; his family has made the wines since. For a sommelier Quintet shows what the Yarra does with Cabernet: perfume, red fruit and fine tannin rather than power.

others.name: Triolet
others.note: The white blend of Sauvignon Blanc, Sémillon and Muscadelle, the white Bordeaux trio, rare in Australia.

traps: Quintet is a Bordeaux blend from Victoria's Yarra Valley, not a Coonawarra or Margaret River wine.

wine.name: Dry Red Wine No. 1
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, much the larger part, with Merlot, Malbec and a little Petit Verdot; the shares move from year to year.
wine.sites: The dry grown estate vineyard at Gruyere, planted from 1969 on a north facing slope of grey silty clay loam banded with gravel; Cabernet and Malbec are of the first plantings, Merlot set among them and more planted, with Petit Verdot, about 1990.
wine.making: The Cabernet is given long skin contact, up to about eight weeks, part of it fermented in a large upright oak cask of three and a half thousand litres. The blend then matures for about fifteen months in French oak barriques, a little over a third of them new in the vintage read, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackberry and blueberry with clove, graphite and a rustic, iodine like note, a thread of dried herb and a little char from the barrel; medium to full in body, with fine, firm tannin.
wine.ageing: Complete enough on release to drink, it is built for the cellar, and the house expects a good vintage to develop for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The house names its reds by number rather than by grape: No. 1 is the Cabernet led blend.
The Geographical Indication on the label, the Victorian region where every grape was grown.

records.table: Yarra Yering's Dry Red Wine No. 1 is a Cabernet led blend from dry grown vines at Gruyere, named by number rather than by grape. Blackberry, clove and graphite over fine, firm tannin, it is made for twenty years in the cellar.
records.story: The estate was founded in 1969 by a scientist rather than a vigneron: a botanist trained in plant physiology who, after a spell of study in Europe, worked for the CSIRO, Australia's national science agency. He chose the ground at Gruyere for its soil and its slope and planted most of the original vineyard in 1969, without irrigation. By the house's account its 1973 vintage was the first commercial wine made in the Yarra Valley since 1921, when the old vineyards had gone. The name of the flagship, as the house tells it, came from the vineyard itself: the first plantings, into block No. 1, were Cabernet vines, and the wine drawn from them became Dry Red Wine No. 1. Its counterpart, Dry Red Wine No. 2, took the Shiraz led blend, and the house has kept to numbered blends rather than varietal labels ever since. Merlot and Petit Verdot were added to the vineyard about 1990. The founder made the wines until the end, and died at the estate on 19 September 2008, after a short illness. For a sommelier No. 1 is the Yarra's revival in a glass, and a lesson in reading a label that names a blend rather than a grape.

wine.name: Yeringberg
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, about three fifths, with Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Malbec and Petit Verdot, grown and picked as a field blend.
wine.sites: The Old Vineyard, replanted from 1969 on the estate's original north east facing slope at Yering, the ground where vines first went in after 1863.
wine.making: The fruit is picked by hand, destemmed and crushed, and fermented in small open tanks with plunging by hand, on its skins for ten days to three weeks. The wine then matures for about twenty one months in French oak barriques, around two fifths of them new in the vintage read.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant, violet, graphite and black olive, with liquorice in riper years; middle weight, fine and perfumed, with supple tannin woven in and a long, fresh finish.
wine.ageing: Supple enough to enjoy within a few years, it gains nuance over a decade, and the house expects good vintages to go much further.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The estate's name alone stands for the red, its Cabernet led blend of the five Bordeaux varieties.
The Geographical Indication on the label, the Victorian region where every grape was grown.

records.table: Yeringberg, the red named simply for the estate, is a Cabernet led field blend from the slope a Swiss settler first planted after 1863. Blackcurrant, violet and graphite at middle weight, with supple tannin, it is a perfumed Yarra red to decant briefly.
records.story: Guillaume de Pury (1831 to 1890), born at Neuchâtel in Switzerland, came to Victoria in 1852 and first tended cattle at Yering, the estate of a fellow Swiss. In 1863, with a partner, he bought part of Yering from its owner's creditors, named it Yeringberg and began a vineyard there; he bought out his partner in 1869. By the heritage register's account the stables and winery followed between 1885 and 1891, a timber building over a stone cellar planned so that grapes and wine moved through it in three dimensions; it stands on the Victorian Heritage Register with its old plant and tools. The valley's table wine lost its market after the First World War, and in 1921 Yeringberg made the last vintage of the old Yarra and pulled out its vines. In 1969 the founder's grandson replanted on the same slope, and the family has made the wines there since; it marked 150 years in 2013. For a sommelier Yeringberg is the Yarra's whole history in one estate: the nineteenth century, the long gap and the revival, on the same ground.

wine.name: Reserve Pinot Noir
wine.sites: Built around the Amphitheatre A Block, a steep north facing slope below the winery planted in 1985, with other estate blocks, such as Coldstream G, added by vintage.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented in small open fermenters of about three tonnes, with a share of whole bunches for perfume and structure. The wine matures for nine to ten months in French oak barrels, about two fifths to a half of them new in the vintages read, before bottling.
wine.glass: Dark cherry, blueberry and cranberry in some years, red cherry and raspberry in others, with a nutmeg like lift from the whole bunches, graphite and wet slate; medium in body, with chalky, persistent tannin.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release, it gains savoury depth over the following decade; the house gives the vintages read a drinking window of a dozen years or so.
wine.serve: 14 to 15 degrees Celsius; no need to decant a young bottle; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The house's selection from its strongest estate blocks, ranked above its Yarra Valley Pinot Noir.
The Geographical Indication on the label; Coldstream is a locality within it, not a region of its own.

records.table: Coldstream Hills Reserve Pinot Noir is the house's selection from the steep Amphitheatre block, planted in 1985 by a wine writer. Cherry, whole bunch lift and chalky tannin at medium weight: pour it a little cool, in a Burgundy glass.
records.story: Coldstream Hills began in 1985, when a Sydney lawyer turned wine writer moved to the Yarra Valley with his wife to make Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. They planted the Amphitheatre and the House Block that year on steep slopes at Coldstream, and the Front Block followed in 1987. By the founder's own account the first vintage, of 1985, was made chiefly from bought grapes, and 1986 was the first of consequence; the winery on the site was built for the 1988 vintage. In 1996 Coldstream Hills was bought by Southcorp, and the founder stayed on for some years as a consultant. Southcorp itself was taken over by Foster's in 2005, and in 2011 Foster's spun its wine business off as Treasury Wine Estates, which took Coldstream Hills with it. The Reserve Pinot Noir is the house's selection from its own blocks, above all the Amphitheatre. For a sommelier it is an early statement of the cool Yarra Pinot Noir that writer turned grower set out to prove.

wine.name: Chandon Vintage Brut
wine.appellation: Australian sparkling wine, its region by vintage
wine.grapes: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, the balance moving with the year; some vintages have also held a little Meunier.
wine.sites: The house's cool, high vineyards in Victoria, above all Whitlands on its high plateau and the Strathbogie Ranges, with Yarra Valley fruit and other cool regions in some years.
wine.making: Made by the traditional method: the base wines are blended and given their second fermentation in the bottle, where the wine rests on its lees for at least two years, three to four in the vintages read, before disgorging; the dosage is low, about five grams a litre in 2019.
wine.glass: White peach, grapefruit zest and strawberry tart over warm pastry and buttered toast from the long lees ageing; a fine, steady bead, crisp acidity and a dry, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink on release after its years on lees; it can be kept a few years more, gaining toast as the fruit recedes.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a tulip shaped white wine glass rather than a narrow flute.

label.means: Every grape was grown in the one year printed on the label; the house has made one every year save 2000 and 2020.
A dry style, with only a small dosage of sugar added after disgorging.

records.table: Chandon's Vintage Brut comes from Moët & Chandon's Australian house at Green Point in the Yarra Valley, by its own account the first wine made there. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from high Victorian vineyards, long on lees, it shows white peach, toast and a crisp, dry finish.
records.story: Chandon Australia grew from the Chandon idea that Moët & Chandon had begun abroad in 1959: traditional method sparkling wine made in the New World by the Champagne house's methods. In the mid 1980s Moët Hennessy's team found its site at Green Point, an old dairy farm at Coldstream, an hour north east of Melbourne in the heart of the Yarra Valley. The house dates itself to 1986, and its first vines at Green Point followed. By the house's account the Vintage Brut was the first wine ever made at Chandon Australia, and it has been made every year since save 2000 and 2020. Long called Domaine Chandon, the house has since written its name Chandon Australia, and its vintage fruit has come increasingly from its own high vineyards at Whitlands and in the Strathbogie Ranges. For a sommelier it is Champagne's method and Champagne's grapes, grown in Victoria and named for no Champagne.
